entries.sentence: The NHS describes heartburn as a burning feeling in the chest caused by stomach acid travelling up towards the throat.
entries.note: NHS page: burning feeling in chest from acid travelling up towards throat; if it keeps happening may be called GORD.

entries.sentence: Besides the burning, people may notice an unpleasant sour taste in the mouth, a hoarse voice or bloating.
entries.note: NHS: heartburn and sour taste; summary also lists hoarse voice, bloating. NHS inform lists bloating, belching, hoarseness, sore throat.

entries.sentence: NHS inform also lists belching, feeling or being sick, a sore throat, and pain or difficulty when swallowing.
entries.note: NHS inform summary lists these other possible signs.

entries.sentence: Not every adult with GERD has heartburn, according to MedlinePlus.
entries.note: Search summary: MedlinePlus says not all adults with GERD have heartburn; attribution to MedlinePlus page not given by url, NIDDK page is closest returned.

entries.sentence: Other reported symptoms include nausea, vomiting, trouble swallowing and tooth wear.
entries.note: Summary of NIDDK/MedlinePlus: nausea, vomiting, swallowing problems and tooth wear.

entries.sentence: The NHS says common triggers include coffee, alcohol, chocolate, smoking, being overweight and some painkillers such as ibuprofen.
entries.note: NHS summary lists these triggers and contributors.

entries.sentence: NIDDK explains that ordinary reflux is stomach contents moving back up into the oesophagus, while GERD is the longer-lasting form that causes repeated symptoms or complications.
entries.note: NIDDK describes GER versus GERD this way.

entries.sentence: NICE describes reflux as a normal process in healthy babies, children and adults.
entries.note: NICE: reflux normal physiological process; GORD when severe enough to merit treatment.

entries.sentence: It is called GORD when the effects are bad enough to need medical treatment.
entries.note: Same NICE summary.

entries.sentence: Easy bringing up of feeds is the typical sign in young babies.
entries.note: Summary: effortless regurgitation of feeds is typical in young babies.

entries.sentence: Worrying features in babies can include poor weight gain, refusing feeds, pain and breathing problems.
entries.note: Search summary listed poor weight gain, refusing feeds, pain, breathing pauses; not attributed to a single page.

entries.sentence: Older children more often have heartburn, and some have asthma, a long-lasting cough or repeated chest infections.
entries.note: Summary: older children more often heartburn; aerodigestive symptoms such as asthma, chronic cough, recurrent pneumonia.

entries.sentence: The summary of NICE advice says not all babies and children need treatment for reflux.
entries.note: Summary: not all children and babies need treatment.

entries.sentence: Advice described includes smaller, more frequent feeds, thickened feeds, avoiding cigarette smoke and placing babies on their backs to sleep.
entries.note: Summary listed these common measures; page-level attribution not certain.

entries.sentence: For most children the outlook is described as good, and babies often improve when weaned onto solids.
entries.note: Summary: most children grow out of it; babies often improve with solids; source page not specified.

entries.sentence: The NHS says tests are not usually needed when the symptoms are typical.
entries.note: Search summary of NHS-affiliated leaflet: tests not usually necessary with typical symptoms; NHS page itself not confirmed to say this.

entries.sentence: If symptoms are severe or medicines do not help, a GP may refer the person to a specialist for tests.
entries.note: Summary: severe or not helped by medicines, GP may refer for tests.

entries.sentence: One test is a gastroscopy, where a thin tube with a camera is passed down the throat to look for the cause.
entries.note: Summary: gastroscopy described this way.

entries.sentence: NIDDK says diagnosis is usually based on symptoms and medical history.
entries.note: Summary of NIDDK/MedlinePlus: diagnosis usually from symptoms and history.

entries.sentence: If symptoms do not improve with lifestyle changes and medicines, further tests such as pH monitoring or endoscopy may be used.
entries.note: Summary: tests such as pH monitoring or endoscopy; one source was a paediatric review, so only partly attributable to NIDDK.

entries.sentence: NHS inform advises seeing a GP if symptoms happen several times a week, over-the-counter medicines are not helping, or there are signs of something more serious such as persistent vomiting, vomiting blood or unexplained weight loss.
entries.note: NHS inform summary of when to see a GP.

entries.sentence: The NHS says a pharmacist can suggest antacids or alginates, which ease symptoms in the short term but do not cure the problem.
entries.note: NHS: antacids and alginates help in short term but will not cure.

entries.sentence: They are not meant to be used regularly for long periods.
entries.note: Summary: should not be taken regularly for long periods.

entries.sentence: A pharmacist can also check whether another medicine, such as an anti-inflammatory painkiller, is making reflux worse.
entries.note: Summary: pharmacists can check other medicines such as ibuprofen.

entries.sentence: If lifestyle changes and pharmacy medicines do not help, the NHS says a GP may prescribe a proton pump inhibitor, a medicine that reduces how much acid the stomach makes.
entries.note: NHS: GP may prescribe a PPI that reduces how much acid the stomach makes.

entries.sentence: If that does not help, a different type called an H2 blocker may be tried.
entries.note: Summary: if PPI does not help, H2 blocker such as famotidine.

entries.sentence: The NHS says surgery is rarely needed.
entries.note: NHS: rarely, surgery is needed.

entries.sentence: NHS inform adds that surgery is considered only if medicines do not control symptoms.
entries.note: NHS inform summary.

entries.sentence: The NHS suggests eating smaller, more frequent meals and avoiding food for a few hours before bed.
entries.note: NHS: smaller more frequent meals; avoid eating within 3 or 4 hours before bed (number omitted).

entries.sentence: It also suggests avoiding tight clothing around the waist, not smoking and not drinking too much alcohol.
entries.note: NHS summary.

entries.sentence: Raising the head of the bed is also suggested, and one NHS page advises against using extra pillows for this because they can strain the tummy.
entries.note: Summary: raising head of bed; one NHS page says extra pillows not to be used; page not specified.

entries.sentence: NIDDK says carrying extra weight may add to symptoms, so a doctor may suggest losing weight.
entries.note: Summary of NIDDK diet page.

entries.sentence: Foods often reported as triggers include citrus fruits, tomatoes, alcohol, chocolate, coffee, high-fat foods, mint and spicy foods.
entries.note: Summary listed these commonly reported triggers.

entries.sentence: NHS inform says heartburn and GORD can often be treated with self-help measures and over-the-counter medicines.
entries.note: NHS inform summary.

entries.sentence: People react differently, so there is no single reflux-friendly diet that suits everyone.
entries.note: Summary: no single diet applies to everyone.

entries.sentence: Long-term acid exposure can cause ulcers, scarring and changes to the cells of the oesophagus.
entries.note: Summary of NHS leaflet content; page attribution approximate.

entries.sentence: Some people develop a stricture, which is a narrowing of the oesophagus.
entries.note: Summary: stricture mentioned.

entries.sentence: Barrett's oesophagus is a change in the lining of the gullet that tends to appear in people with reflux.
entries.note: Summary: change in lining of gullet in people with reflux.

entries.sentence: One NHS leaflet says it does not usually cause symptoms beyond those of GORD, so people with it are usually followed up with endoscopy.
entries.note: Summary: Barrett's usually no extra symptoms; surveillance with endoscopy.

entries.sentence: NHS information says the longer someone has Barrett's oesophagus, the higher the lifetime risk of cancer.
entries.note: Summary: a separate NHS source says this.

entries.sentence: NHS inform links a hiatus hernia with an impaired valve that normally keeps acid in the stomach.
entries.note: Summary attributed hiatus hernia link to an NHS source; exact page uncertain.

entries.sentence: Some people still have symptoms despite standard treatment with proton pump inhibitors, which is why further assessment is sometimes needed.
entries.note: Summary of a 2023 review: persistent symptoms despite PPIs; not NIDDK, so attribution approximate.

entries.sentence: The NHS describes heartburn as the burning feeling in the chest from acid travelling up towards the throat.
entries.note: NHS page wording.

entries.sentence: If it keeps happening, it may be called gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, or GORD.
entries.note: NHS page wording.

entries.sentence: So heartburn is the symptom, and GORD is the longer-lasting condition behind it.
entries.note: NHS page wording.

entries.sentence: The NHS says antacids and alginates ease symptoms in the short term but will not cure the problem.
entries.note: NHS page statements.

entries.sentence: They are not meant to be used regularly for long periods.
entries.note: NHS page statements.

entries.sentence: A pharmacist can advise, and a GP can discuss stronger medicines if lifestyle changes and pharmacy medicines are not helping.
entries.note: NHS page statements.

entries.sentence: No.
entries.note: Summary of NHS-affiliated leaflet and page.

entries.sentence: Tests are not usually needed when symptoms are typical.
entries.note: Summary of NHS-affiliated leaflet and page.

entries.sentence: If symptoms are severe, or medicines do not help, a GP may refer the person for a gastroscopy, where a thin tube with a camera is passed down the throat to look for the cause.
entries.note: Summary of NHS-affiliated leaflet and page.

entries.sentence: Reflux is a normal process in healthy babies, and summaries of NHS and NICE information say most children grow out of it.
entries.note: Search summary of children's reflux sources; page-level attribution approximate.

entries.sentence: Babies often improve when they start solid food.
entries.note: Search summary of children's reflux sources; page-level attribution approximate.

entries.sentence: Treatment matters more if a child is not growing well or has other symptoms, and a clinician can assess this.
entries.note: Search summary of children's reflux sources; page-level attribution approximate.

entries.sentence: The NHS says to seek advice if lifestyle changes and pharmacy medicines are not helping, if heartburn happens most days, or if there is food sticking in the throat, frequent sickness or weight loss for no reason.
entries.note: NHS and NHS inform lists. The 999 part restates the existing entry's seekCare, not newly sourced.

entries.sentence: A GP appointment is the usual route; for vomiting blood or collapse, call 999.
entries.note: NHS and NHS inform lists. The 999 part restates the existing entry's seekCare, not newly sourced.

entries.sentence: Acid reflux, GORD, GERD, heartburn (when the burning chest feeling is the main symptom)
entries.note: NHS page names heartburn, acid reflux, GORD.

entries.sentence: Burning in the chest, sour taste in the mouth, sometimes hoarse voice or bloating
entries.note: NHS page.

entries.sentence: Smaller, more frequent meals; not eating just before bed; not smoking; pharmacist advice
entries.note: NHS self-care list.

entries.sentence: Antacids and alginates ease symptoms short term but do not cure
entries.note: NHS.

entries.sentence: A GP may prescribe a proton pump inhibitor, then an H2 blocker if needed
entries.note: NHS.

entries.sentence: Often none for typical symptoms; gastroscopy if severe or not responding
entries.note: Summary of NHS-affiliated leaflet.

entries.note: NHS: rarely, surgery is needed.
